components.text: The decisive demand is whether consolation compromises truthfulness or divine-command claims deny innate human moral agency.
Whether religious commitment is accepted as consolation at the expense of intellectual integrity.
Whether moral discrimination must come only from divine command rather than innate human agency.
The decisive demand is whether Christianity's authoritative structure characteristically supplies coercion rather than a norm capable of restraining it.
Whether divine surveillance, compulsory obedience, and punishment make monotheistic authority structurally coercive.
The decisive demand is whether natural history makes Christian revelation intellectually untenable rather than merely contestable.
Whether long natural history, suffering, and late localized intervention undermine Christian revelation.
The decisive demand is whether innate human moral discrimination makes divine or transcendent grounding unnecessary.
Whether innate human moral discrimination is sufficient without a transcendent source of obligation.
The decisive demand is whether beneficial religious conduct establishes Christianity's truth or benign general moral character.
Whether Jesus's nonviolent norm can criticize violent Christians and inspire concrete forgiveness.
The decisive demand is whether a transcendent basis is needed to make moral action or obligation viable.
Whether secular moral systems can justify binding obligation without a transcendent moral foundation.
The decisive demand is whether Christianity's internal nonviolent norm distinguishes religious pathology from secular ideological atrocities.
Whether Christianity contains an internal nonviolent norm capable of criticizing violent adherents.
The decisive demand is whether psychological consolation undermines religious truthfulness or human moral integrity.
Whether a consoling desire for religious belief undermines its truth or the believer's intellectual integrity.
The decisive demand is whether Christian redemption necessarily transfers guilt through punitive sacrifice and erases personal responsibility.
Whether Christian redemption requires morally objectionable punishment that transfers or erases another person's responsibility.
The decisive demand is whether secular resources can sustain viable moral obligation without a transcendent foundation.
Whether moral obligation can remain viable without a transcendent basis that authorizes or secures it.
The decisive demand is whether scientific natural history excludes or substantially discredits transcendent religious explanation.
A further demand is whether naturalistic explanation exhausts meaning and value as well as material causal relations.
Whether natural history, suffering, and delayed localized revelation count against Christian intervention claims.
Whether evolved solidarity and reciprocity can sustain moral obligation without supernatural assumptions.
The decisive demand is whether difficult scriptural material must be treated as timeless divine authorization of violence.
A further demand is whether claimed divine authority leaves adherents no principled internal basis for resisting coercive commands.
Whether Christian redemption makes another person's punishment erase the wrongdoer's moral responsibility.
Whether claimed divine authority remains coercive through compulsory obedience, surveillance, and punishment.
The decisive demand is whether Christian authority promotes coercion and dehumanization rather than restraining them.
A further demand is whether religious habits characteristically intensify ideological violence and obedience.
Whether religious alliances and transferred habits of faith and obedience answer comparisons with secular atrocities.
The decisive demand is whether conceptual room for transcendence warrants confident Christian claims about revelation and divine commands.
A further demand is whether scientific underdetermination places Christian interpretation on adequate evidential footing.
A further demand is whether a claimed revelatory lens can justify knowledge of specific divine intentions and commands.
Whether scientific limits leave transcendent meaning as a legitimate complementary religious interpretation.
Whether nature's openness to several worldviews leaves Christian interpretation epistemically available.
